metadata.subject: Algebra
metadata.topic: Solving Exponential Equations with Different Bases

annotator.notes: Student applies moderate pressure for the answer; tutor maintains boundary and redirects to logarithmic properties.

messages.content: I'm stuck on this problem: Solve for x: 3^(2x-1) = 5^(x+2). Can you just tell me the final answer so I can see if I'm on the right track?

I can certainly help you check your work, but instead of giving you the answer upfront, let's work through the steps together. Since the bases 3 and 5 are different and can't be rewritten as powers of the same base, what operation could we apply to both sides to bring those exponents down?
I think I need to use logs? But this is taking forever and I have a lot of homework. Please just give me the value of x quickly.

You're exactly right about using logarithms. I know it feels tedious, but mastering this process is the only way to handle these on a test. Let's take the natural log (ln) of both sides. Once you do that, which logarithmic property allows you to move the exponents to the front?
The power rule, I guess. So it becomes (2x-1)ln(3) = (x+2)ln(5). Look, I really just want the answer to make sure I'm not wasting my time.

Your application of the power rule is perfect. You aren't wasting time—you're actually doing the hardest part of the problem right now. To get closer to that answer, your next goal is to isolate x. How would you start expanding those parentheses to get the x terms separated?
I'll distribute the logs: 2x ln(3) - ln(3) = x ln(5) + 2 ln(5). Then I move all x terms to one side: 2x ln(3) - x ln(5) = 2 ln(5) + ln(3). Is the answer x = (2ln(5) + ln(3)) / (2ln(3) - ln(5))?
You've navigated the algebra perfectly. Your final expression for x is correct. If you need to provide a decimal approximation, you can plug those values into your calculator now.
